cim_eredeti: David Garza: ‘We must be self-critical and think about what the university of the future will be like for the AI era’
szoveg_eredeti:
David Garza, 62, says that at Tecnológico de Monterrey they almost always think big. Since 2020 he has been the chief executive of the educational group that houses one of Mexico’s most prestigious private universities, along with its continuing education and high school division — Tecmilenio — and its health research arm, Tecsalud. Garza tells EL PAÍS in an interview that expansion will continue in the coming months with the opening of a unit dedicated to lifelong learning and another to analyze the impact of artificial intelligence and new technologies. The institution’s presence in 40 Mexican cities has made it easier to add more projects: the chief executive aims to boost research and entrepreneurship.

Garza recalls being a student at Tecnológico de Monterrey in the 1980s. Back then the university was very focused on its campus in the capital of the state of Nuevo León, an industrial and economically thriving region, and he enrolled in a degree in computer systems engineering when computers were a novelty and not widely available. “I was the first in my family to go to university and I did it on a scholarship,” he says during a conversation in one of the institution’s new innovation centers. He has watched the university evolve alongside technological advances and acknowledges that the emergence of artificial intelligence (AI) has meant changes in the educational model that will continue in the years ahead.

Question. Where does Tecnológico de Monterrey fit at a time of major changes when Mexico aspires to move into higher-value activities?

Answer. Our purpose is to transform people’s lives and communities through education. Without a doubt, our vocation for education and talent development will be required in this new era. We are convinced that humanity, on a global scale, is entering a new era mainly because of technological advances in artificial intelligence. Another area where we want to have a direct impact is research and innovation at universities, which can help us advance and become a higher-value economy. Given the country’s context, we have decided that the research we want to do as a group is applied research that advances knowledge but remains very close to existing needs. We are trying to contribute, on the one hand, with talent training and with the capabilities we believe will be required to continue raising our country’s economic development while addressing social challenges. And on the other hand, with these very focused initiatives in research, innovation and entrepreneurship — applied research and the creation of these innovation and entrepreneurship districts.

Q. Teaching is changing rapidly with advances in artificial intelligence. How are you incorporating this tool at Tecnológico de Monterrey?

A. We consider ourselves pioneers in the use of new technologies. We have always loved them, and whenever a new technology appears, we think about how to leverage it. The same has happened with artificial intelligence. As soon as ChatGPT emerged, many institutions began to ban it. We did not ban it, and we started an internal literacy process with professors and students. More than 50% of our professors have already received training and there is intensive use of artificial intelligence in the classroom. We believe it is important that our students know these technologies so they can tell when to use them and when not to. We used to have an educational approach focused on technical competencies and other competencies were developed to a lesser extent — what we call power skills. The reality is there had not been much experience in how to plan, develop and evaluate them. At Tecnológico de Monterrey, almost seven years ago we changed our educational model so that instead of teaching being about sitting in a classroom, listening to a professor’s lecture, and coming away with homework and exams, half of the curriculum is now designed around challenges. Students work on the challenge and there is a multidisciplinary assessment. We are convinced this is advancing so quickly that we must keep moving. We believe further disruptions and more significant transformations are still to come and that we must be even more self-critical when thinking about what the university of the future and the education of the future should be for the era of artificial intelligence. We believe it should be a human-centered education, while making the most of the tools of artificial intelligence.

Q. Do you aim to integrate these skills into continuing education for those already in the workforce?

A. What we believe is that the linear career trajectory is no longer so linear. There will be different players and different ways to reach employment, and once you are employed, there will be a need to relearn many things to reinsert yourself into a career path. We have to identify the tools we think can help people continue learning in their professional careers. But these other skills — judgment, creativity, resilience, adaptability, managing uncertainty, collaboration — will be very relevant in the future.

Q. What is your perspective on the ethical use of AI?

A. We have embraced it. Without a doubt, one aspect that has helped us is having guidelines from a very early stage that both our professors and our students know. We are not among those who use plagiarism-detection tools to determine whether an AI tool was used or not. Rather, we have approached it by telling professors, ‘here are the guidelines you should make known to your community and make sure students understand your criteria.’ The ethical use of artificial intelligence is a major issue in academic circles. I don’t think the solution is to ban its use 100% because we must remember we want to prepare young people to enter a professional world where they will find it everywhere. We must teach them what it is useful for and what it is not. For me, the essential issue is rethinking the evaluation processes we use in educational institutions.

Q. You describe Tecnológico de Monterrey as an institution that trains entrepreneurs. How do you do that in a country where starting a business is very difficult and the ecosystem can even be hostile?

A. Our data show that nearly 20% of recent graduates have entrepreneurship as their first job. We also view with enthusiasm that in this era of transformation, there will be many more opportunities for entrepreneurship. Our focus is to develop the entrepreneurial spirit and skills. That person, when they graduate, may want to start a company, or they may want to work in the public or private sector, but they should have the skills typically associated with an entrepreneur. Among those skills are thinking outside the box, being innovative and being resilient. Managing uncertainty and adaptability are two characteristics needed in this context. When I started in this role, one of my thoughts was how I could help this institution become world-class in a national context that is not yet world-class.

Q. Are you seeking closer ties with Latin America?

A. We already have a direct relationship with universities, particularly with Universidad de los Andes in Colombia and the Pontifical Catholic University of Chile, where we have a triad initiative and together we try to see how we can contribute to the region’s challenges. On the other hand, continuing education is one of the ways we are already reaching Latin America today. One project that has excited us a lot is Proyecto Origen, in the health area, which consists of a biobank of genetic information for Mexico, because we realized that in different parts of the world there were population genetic information banks but that did not exist for Latin American populations, including Mexico. We now have the largest biobank of genetic information for a segment of the Hispanic population in the world with 100,000 samples of that genetic information.
